title: Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital
subtitle: Meng Yuanlao · Recalling Northern Song Bianliang · Dreaming Back 150 Years of Glory
description: Meng Yuanlao, bearing the sobriquet Youlan Jushi, was a man of the late Northern Song and early Southern Song whose life details are largely unknown. After the Jingkang Incident, he fled south and took up residence in Jiangnan. In the seventeenth year of the Shaoxing reign (1147), recalling the past splendor of the former capital Bianliang, he wrote the ten-volume Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital, meticulously recording the palaces, markets, taverns, temples, gardens, festivals, and folk customs of the Northern Song's Eastern Capital (present-day Kaifeng). This is a work written to resist oblivion through memory—when the old capital lay in ruins, only words could bring it back to life. This route steps into Meng Yuanlao's Bianliang, seeking out that dreamed-of Eastern Capital in present-day Kaifeng.

route.title: Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital: Dreaming Back to Northern Song Bianliang, In Search of a Lost City of Splendor
route.intro:
Peace had reigned so long that the people flourished. Children knew only how to dance and play; the gray-haired elders had never known the clang of weapons.
Meng Yuanlao spent his youth in the Eastern Capital (present-day Kaifeng). In those days, Bianliang was the most prosperous metropolis on earth—with a population exceeding one million, several times larger than any European city of the same era. The Bian River was thronged daily with grain-transport boats; the Great Xiangguo Temple hosted five "market days for a myriad households" each month; when the Golden Bright Pool opened in spring, "the entire city turned out to behold it"—Meng Yuanlao grew up in a city of dazzling color and light. In the second year of the Jingkang reign (1127), the Jin army captured Bianliang, and the Northern Song fell. Meng Yuanlao, together with countless refugees, fled south, gazing at unfamiliar mountains and waters in a strange land. He spent twenty years preparing himself, and finally, in the seventeenth year of the Shaoxing reign (1147), he took up his brush and wrote down his memories of the Eastern Capital, stroke by stroke. He wrote not of politics, not of military affairs, but of the life of the streets—the little stalls, the taverns, the tea houses, the temple fairs, the festivals—because he knew that this was the soul of a city. Let us open Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital and step into that Eastern Capital of Bianliang, a place that could only be returned to in dreams.

stops.title: Stop One: The Imperial Palace—The Past Life of the Forbidden City
stops.content: The first volume of Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital describes the Imperial Palace—the Song emperor's palace complex. Meng Yuanlao wrote: "The main gate of the Imperial Palace, the Xuande Tower, has five portals, each with golden nails and vermilion lacquer, the walls built with brick and stone, carved with dragons, phoenixes, and drifting clouds"—golden nails, vermilion gates, dragon and phoenix carvings—luxury at its most extreme. The Imperial Avenue before Xuande Tower was two hundred paces wide, flanked by "imperial ditches" planted with lotus, and banks lined with peach, plum, apricot, and pear trees—when spring brought the blossoms, the entire street was drenched in fragrance. This Northern Song imperial palace has long been buried several meters deep beneath successive floods of the Yellow River. But on its site, the Dragon Pavilion, a Qing-dynasty hall built on the ruins of the Song and Jin palaces, now stands. From the Dragon Pavilion, looking down over Kaifeng, you stand where the Northern Song emperors once held court. This hall has witnessed a millennium of dynastic change from the Song to the Qing—the Northern Song perished in the Jingkang Incident, and the Qing dynasty continued the imagination of former dynasties on Dragon Pavilion. Though Meng Yuanlao's "Imperial Palace" has vanished, the Pan and Yang Lakes before the Dragon Pavilion—legend says Pan Lake is turbid and Yang Lake is clear—still silently tell the tale of loyal and treacherous ministers. In describing the Imperial Palace in Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital, Meng Yuanlao's every word and phrase carries reverence. He wrote that the Xuande Tower had "five portals, each with golden nails and vermilion lacquer"—forty-nine golden nails on each door, two hundred and forty-five in total, glittering in the sunlight. The Imperial Avenue before the tower was "about two hundred paces wide"—converted from Song measurements, nearly three hundred meters, broader than today's Chang'an Avenue. The "imperial ditches" on either side of the avenue were planted with lotus, "when summer lotus bloomed, the fragrance could be smelled for miles." Meng Yuanlao recorded these delicate sensory memories because he knew that this was what the true "Eastern Capital" was made of. The core building of the Imperial Palace was the Hall of Great Celebration—"whenever a great ritual was held, the emperor fasted here, and New Year's Day court audiences were held here." The hall spanned nine bays in width and five in depth, roofed with yellow glazed tiles, and before it stood a sundial and a standard measure—symbols of imperial authority over time and space. Meng Yuanlao noted a particular detail: the "Dragon Stairs" before the Hall of Great Celebration were carved with cloud-dragon patterns, "after rain, when the sky cleared, the dragons seemed to come alive"—the dragons on the rain-washed stone stairs appeared ready to break out of the stone. This ability to find poetry in the mundane is what makes Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital most remarkable. Meng Yuanlao also wrote about the "people's wards" beyond the Imperial Palace—the residential areas of commoners. "Within the Eastern Capital there were one hundred and thirty-six wards," each with a gate and a ward chief (equivalent to today's neighborhood committee director), and the ward gates were closed at night—"when the evening drum sounded three hundred times, all ward gates were shut." But the prosperity of the Eastern Capital made the curfew system a dead letter—Meng Yuanlao wrote that "the night market lasted until the third watch, and by the fifth watch it opened again"—it was practically a city that never slept. From the golden nails and vermilion doors of the Hall of Great Celebration to the pancake stalls of the wards, Meng Yuanlao measured the entire Eastern Capital with his brush—from the emperor's golden throne to the common people's kitchen stove.

stops.title: Stop Two: The Great Xiangguo Temple—A Buddhist Market for a Myriad Households
stops.content: The Xiangguo Temple occupies a major portion of Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital. Originally the mansion of the Warring States figure Lord Xinling, the temple became the largest Buddhist monastery and the most important commercial center of the Northern Song's Eastern Capital. Meng Yuanlao wrote: "The Xiangguo Temple opens five times each month, for a myriad households to trade"—on the first, eighth, fifteenth, eighteenth, and twenty-eighth of each month, the temple gates would open, and merchants and citizens from all over the city would swarm in, setting up stalls before the Buddha hall to buy and sell. Anything could be bought at the temple: birds and beasts, household goods, antiques, calligraphy and paintings... incense burned inside the Buddha hall while haggling went on outside—this wondrous blend of "sacred and secular" is a vivid portrait of Northern Song civil society. Meng Yuanlao even recorded which stalls sold what: woven bamboo mats in the courtyard, preserved fruits and pastries near the Buddha hall... such meticulousness reveals how deeply he missed these ordinary scenes of bustle. Today's Xiangguo Temple remains a Buddhist center in Kaifeng. Though its scale cannot compare with the past, when you enter its gates, you can vaguely understand Meng Yuanlao's words: "All the arts and crafts are gathered here"—a single temple is the epitome of an entire city. When Meng Yuanlao wrote about the temple's "market for a myriad households," his brushstrokes are as excited as a child's. He recorded every district's specialty: "On the great triple gate are all kinds of birds and cats, rare birds and strange beasts, none lacking"—live animals near the mountain gate; "On the second and third gates are all household utensils, the courtyard set up with colored awnings, open stalls, and makeshift shops"—household goods area; "Near the Buddha hall, the honeyed preserves of Wang Daoren of the Meng family compound, Zhao Wenxiu's brushes, Pan Gu's ink"—near the Buddha hall was the premium cultural products section, and he even remembered the merchants' names. "On both side corridors, nuns from various temples sell embroidery, collars, flowers, pearls, and hair ornaments"—the side corridors were the nuns' "handicraft boutique." This model of "temple plus shopping mall" is probably unique in world history. The Xiangguo Temple's "market for a myriad households" flourished thanks to the explosive growth of the Northern Song's commodity economy. Kaifeng's permanent population at this time exceeded one million, and including the floating population, may have reached nearly one and a half million—while contemporary London had fewer than twenty thousand. In a city of such scale, this market was the inevitable release of consumer desire by the citizen class. The Bian River's grain transport ensured the supply of goods—every year, six million shi of grain were shipped into Kaifeng via the Bian River (equivalent to about 450 million jin)—"the Bian River is to the capital what blood vessels are to the body." Meng Yuanlao's Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital was no fairy tale—it was a record of a city civilization that was among the first to step through the door of modernity.

stops.title: Stop Three: Rainbow Bridge and the Bian River—The Golden Waterway of Along the River During the Qingming Festival
stops.content: The Bian River was the lifeline of the Eastern Capital. Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital records: "The Bian River diverts water from the Luo River at the Western Capital and enters the capital, flowing east to Si Prefecture and into the Huai River." This man-made canal carried grain, silk, and ceramics from Jiangnan ceaselessly to the capital. In Meng Yuanlao's writing, the banks of the Bian River were the most bustling part of the Eastern Capital: "On both banks are singing pavilions and wine shops, bustling even past midnight." Once spanning the Bian River was a famous Rainbow Bridge—the wooden arched bridge teeming with people in Zhang Zeduan's painting Along the River During the Qingming Festival. The Rainbow Bridge had no piers, relying on an arching wooden framework—a marvel of Song engineering. Unfortunately, the Rainbow Bridge no longer exists; the Yellow River's floods buried the entire Northern Song Eastern Capital underground. But the Northern Song Eastern Capital Site (including Bo Pagoda and Yanqing Temple) is now a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level, and archaeologists are gradually excavating that buried city. Standing on the banks of the Bian River today, the waterway is far narrower than in its prime. But close your eyes, and you can still hear the boat trackers' chants and the pipa of tavern songstresses—isn't that how Meng Yuanlao "heard" them? The pages of Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital describing the Bian River read like a textual version of Along the River During the Qingming Festival. Meng Yuanlao wrote: "On both banks of the Bian River are singing pavilions and wine shops"—the most famous being the "Tower of Bountiful Joy," "five towers facing each other, each with flying bridges and balustrades, connected in light and shadow." This was a mega-entertainment complex of five buildings linked by skywalks, "with pearl blinds and embroidered canopies, lanterns and candles dazzling." The scale of the Tower of Bountiful Joy was astonishing—"each tower has a dozen small chambers," receiving "no fewer than a thousand guests" daily. Locals called dining there "going up the tall tower"—the equivalent of a three-Michelin-star restaurant today. The Rainbow Bridge was the most stunning engineering marvel on the Bian River. Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital records: "The Rainbow Bridge has no pillars; it is entirely framed from massive timbers, decorated with red paint, like a flying rainbow." This pierless arched bridge relied entirely on the interlocking mortise and tenon joints of wooden beams, spanning over twenty meters. The bridge depicted by Zhang Zeduan in Along the River During the Qingming Festival was this very Rainbow Bridge—people jostling shoulder to shoulder above, grain boats passing through the arch below, the tense moment when "the mast is about to touch the bridge but hasn't yet" captured perfectly by the painter. Meng Yuanlao with words, Zhang Zeduan with paint—two men expressing their love for the same city through different media: every corner of the Eastern Capital was worth remembering.

stops.title: Stop Four: Golden Bright Pool—Spring Revelry in an Imperial Garden
stops.content: Golden Bright Pool (Jinming Chi) was an imperial garden west of the Northern Song Eastern Capital, opened to the public every spring. Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital devotes an entire volume to the bustle of Golden Bright Pool: "On the first day of the third month, Golden Bright Pool and Qionglin Garden open... from the first of the third month to the eighth of the fourth month when the pool closes, even in wind and rain there are visitors." Each spring, the emperor watched naval exercises and dragon boat races at Golden Bright Pool, while commoners "turned out en masse to behold them"—this was the biggest annual carnival in the Eastern Capital. Meng Yuanlao wrote of the Waterside Palace by the pool—where the emperor sat to watch the dragon boats; of the Immortal Bridge—a vermilion arched bridge; and of the Water-Heart Pavilion in the middle of the pool—only reachable by boat. "Carriages and horses throng, one cannot stand still"—the crowds were so dense you couldn't hold your ground, swept along by the tide of people. Today, Golden Bright Pool is a historical name—the Song-era gardens and ponds have all been erased by the repeated floods of the Yellow River. But the words of Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital have preserved it forever on paper—"Though several hundred years have passed, the record is so detailed that reading it makes you feel as if you are witnessing it yourself"—this was probably the tribute Meng Yuanlao most wanted to hear. Meng Yuanlao's chapter on Golden Bright Pool is the happiest passage in all of Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital. He described the grand opening: "From the first day of the third month to the eighth of the fourth month when the pool closes, even in wind and rain there are visitors, scarcely a day goes by without crowds"—a full thirty-nine days, regardless of weather, the poolside was never quiet. The emperor watched the dragon boat races from the Waterside Palace—"over twenty dragon boats, each with a dragon head at the prow and a dragon tail at the stern," the oarsmen "all dressed in red," drums shaking the sky. Meng Yuanlao also noted the food stalls by the pool: "Those selling snacks set up tents under the willow shade"—when tired, you could sit and have a bowl of "plum and ginger soup" or a serving of "grilled pig skin." The architecture of Golden Bright Pool displayed the finest touches of Song imperial garden design. In the center of the pool stood the "Water-Heart Pavilion"—"the pool is built of stone, with a hall in the middle," only reachable by ferry, where the emperor entertained ministers. The Immortal Bridge connecting the pavilion to the shore—"vermiculium railings, green tiles, winding and twisting"—was a paradigm of Song garden bridge architecture. None of these structures remain today, but the Kaifeng City Wall—14.4 kilometers of Ming-Qing fortifications—still stands in the old city. Gazing at the cityscape from atop the wall, you can still feel the kind of civic vitality that Meng Yuanlao described. And on the bustling old streets, the Shan-Shaan-Gan Guild Hall, with its exquisite brick, wood, and stone carvings, represents the flowering of Northern Song Bianliang's commercial spirit in the Qing dynasty—from Meng Yuanlao to the Shanxi merchants, Kaifeng's prosperity simply continued in a different form.

stops.title: Stop Five: Iron Pagoda and Bo Pagoda—Kaifeng's Millennial Guardians
stops.content: After repeated Yellow River floods and wartime destruction had leveled nearly all of the Northern Song's buildings, two pagodas miraculously survived in Kaifeng. The first is the Youguo Temple Pagoda—commonly called the "Iron Pagoda" because its outer walls are entirely covered in brown glazed tiles, giving it the appearance of iron from a distance. Built in the first year of the Northern Song Huangyou reign (1049), it is octagonal, thirteen stories, and fifty-five meters tall. When the Yellow River flooded, the pagoda's base was buried several meters deep in silt, but the tower itself stood motionless—it has watched nearly a thousand Kaifeng sunrises and sunsets. The second is the Bo Pagoda (part of the Northern Song Eastern Capital Site), nearly a century older than the Iron Pagoda. Bo Pagoda originally had nine stories, but during the Yuan dynasty the upper six were destroyed by lightning. In the Ming, a small pagoda was built on top of the remaining three, creating the unique spectacle of "a pagoda on a pagoda." Meng Yuanlao did not write specifically about these two pagodas in Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital—perhaps because they were so common in his day as to seem unremarkable. But today, they are the only intact buildings from the Northern Song Eastern Capital. Gazing up at the Iron Pagoda, you can feel with the utmost reality that the Eastern Capital of Meng Yuanlao's dreams once truly existed. The construction of Youguo Temple Pagoda (Iron Pagoda) represents the pinnacle of Song engineering: 55.08 meters tall, octagonal, thirteen stories, the brown glazed tiles covering its exterior come in twenty-eight different shapes—each specially fired. Each layer features brick-carved imitation-wood brackets, rafters, and eaves tiles, the most exquisite being the glazed tiles engraved with more than fifty patterns including flying apsaras, descending dragons, qilin, and bodhisattvas—"towering aloft, poised as if in flight." People of old thought the pagoda was made of iron—hence the name—but it is actually a glazed-brick pagoda; its brown glaze merely resembles rust. In the late Yuan and early Ming, the Yellow River repeatedly flooded, burying Kaifeng several meters deep, and the Iron Pagoda's base was also submerged—"the Iron Pagoda walks among the clouds," it seems to rise straight out of the earth. The story of Bo Pagoda is even stranger. Built in the seventh year of the Northern Song Kaibao reign (974), over seventy years older than the Iron Pagoda, it is Kaifeng's oldest surviving structure. The original nine-story pagoda lost six stories to a Yuan-dynasty lightning strike. The Ming built a seven-story miniature pagoda atop the remaining three—thus was the wonder of "pagoda upon pagoda" born. The pagoda's inner and outer walls are covered with brick Buddhas—"one brick, one Buddha," 6,923 in total, each with slightly different expressions and hand gestures—a veritable "wall of ten thousand Buddhas." Entering the pagoda, in the dim light, the Bodhisattva images sit serenely on every wall, a thousand years of quiet presence. The overwhelming sense of "ten thousand Buddhas in one cave" inevitably recalls Meng Yuanlao's words: "All the arts and crafts are gathered here"—everything about the Eastern Capital was born from consummate craftsmanship.

stops.title: Stop Six: Yanqing Temple—The Jade Emperor Pavilion of a Yuan-Dynasty Daoist Temple
stops.content: Meng Yuanlao's Eastern Capital held not only Buddhist temples but also Daoist temples. And Kaifeng's most extraordinary existing ancient structure—the Jade Emperor Pavilion in Yanqing Temple (part of the Northern Song Eastern Capital Site)—was built in the Yuan dynasty, yet on that land described by Meng Yuanlao, it continued the Daoist incense tradition. Yanqing Temple was built to commemorate Wang Chongyang, the founder of the Quanzhen school of Daoism. The Jade Emperor Pavilion is entirely covered in glazed tiles, shimmering in sunlight. Inside, the Jade Emperor is enshrined, and the walls are covered with Daoist murals—immortals with flowing robes and ribbons, so vivid they seem about to step off the wall. This kind of Yuan-dynasty Daoist architecture is rare in all of China; that Kaifeng should harbor such a treasure is reason enough for Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital to be endlessly fond of this city. After completing Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital in the seventeenth year of the Shaoxing reign, Meng Yuanlao never returned to Kaifeng. He spent the rest of his life in Jiangnan, watching the misty rain over West Lake by day while his heart yearned for the sound of the Bian River at night. In his preface, he wrote: "The ancients spoke of dreaming of the Land of Huaxu, where joy knew no bounds. Now I look back, and my heart is filled with longing." He named his book "Dreams of Splendor" because all of it was indeed like a dream.
